elements.quote:
However, studies assessing their effectiveness in delivering primary prevention interventions for non-communicable disease prevention and control in LMIC settings are limited,[10] though this has been proven for developed countries.[11]
Further, whatever sparse results are available are mostly through observational studies and evidence from controlled trials needs to be synthesised.
Only four systematic reviews assessing this effectiveness in LMIC/ developing countries could be identified after review of published literature.[11-14]
elements.reason: The current knowledge is described as limited/sparse, but the evidence provided does not clearly articulate specific “important uncertainties” beyond stating that effectiveness parameters need synthesis.

elements.quote: Considering this deficiency in availability of effectiveness parameters, a systematic review on effectiveness of CHW delivered primary prevention interventions for NCDs in developing countries was conducted by the authors.
elements.reason: The need for conducting the review is explicitly explained as addressing a deficiency in available effectiveness parameters.

elements.quote: Only four systematic reviews assessing this effectiveness in LMIC/ developing countries could be identified after review of published literature.[11-14]
elements.reason: The existence of similar systematic reviews is acknowledged (though the evidence does not specify updates/replications or cite a specific previous review as the motivation for a new review beyond noting how many were found).

elements.quote: This was conducted following the hypothesis that for NCD control programs employing a community health worker is more likely to be successful than routine care.
elements.reason: A hypothesised rationale/mechanistic expectation is stated: CHW-delivered programs are hypothesised to be more successful than routine care.
No logic model depicting hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes is reported in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence does not provide an explicit statement of the review objective(s) or question(s) in a question-formulation framework.

elements.quote: Binary outcomes were reported as relative risk (RR) of outcomes in the intervention group compared to the control group. For continuous outcomes, and where baseline data were available, mean difference (MD) between the change in the intervention and control groups were reported.
elements.reason: The evidence indicates the presence of intervention vs control comparisons in effect estimation, but it does not explicitly state the planned comparisons using PICO (or an appropriate variant) for the review.

elements.quote: A research was considered eligible for inclusion if it followed a randomised controlled study design in community settings of low middle income countries with community health worker as intervention delivery person for general or high risk population for primary prevention of NCDs as compared to routine care or enhanced routine care as comparator.
elements.reason: The eligibility characteristics are specified for study design (randomised controlled; community settings; CHW intervention; general/high-risk population; primary prevention of NCDs; comparator routine/enhanced routine care). However, the evidence provided does not specify any follow-up requirements.

elements.quote: Only randomised controlled trials (community based randomised controlled trial, cluster randomised trials) published in the last 15 years (2000-2015) were included in the review. ... without restriction to language:
elements.reason: Dissemination year (2000–2015) and language (no restriction) are specified. The evidence does not clearly state eligibility criteria for publication/report status (e.g., what counts as eligible published vs unpublished reports).
No evidence was found describing whether exclusions were distinguished between cases where outcomes were not measured versus cases where outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: Outcomes of interventions identified under the review were grouped into health topics identified in the protocol. ... Meta-analyses were carried out separately for each outcome and type of study design (RCT/ cRCT).
elements.reason: The evidence describes how outcomes were grouped (health topics) and that meta-analyses were done separately by outcome and study design (RCT/cRCT), but it does not explicitly link these groups to the specific comparisons defined in the review objectives.
Although time period and design restrictions are described, the evidence provided does not give rationales specifically for notable restrictions on study eligibility (as required).

elements.quote: PubMed (20002015); Excerpta Medica Database (EMBASE) (2000-2015); OVID (2000-2015) and World PLOS Health Organization (WHO) library and Cochrane library.
elements.reason: The evidence reports coverage years (e.g., 2000-2015) for some sources, but it does not report the specific date when each source was last searched or consulted.

elements.quote: Searches of published literature on effectiveness of NCD control interventions delivered through community health worker under the programme (focus on developing countries) were done in the following biomedical, and general reference electronic databases, without restriction to language: PubMed (20002015); Excerpta Medica Database (EMBASE) (2000-2015); OVID (2000-2015) and World PLOS Health Organization (WHO) library and Cochrane library.
elements.reason: Names and year coverage ranges are given for bibliographic databases, but the search interface/platform is not specified.

elements.quote: Clinical trials registers such as ClinicalTrials.gov and portals to trials registers of different developing countries through (World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, ICTRP) [20] were another source of information that were reviewed for relevant literature.
elements.reason: The registers/platform names are provided (ClinicalTrials.gov, ICTRP), but date restrictions for these registers are not clearly reported in this excerpt.

elements.quote: Website of the Health-Evidence.org was referred to for related reviews.
elements.reason: The website name is given, but the URL is not reported.
The evidence mentions contacting authors or trial investigators, but does not name any organisations or manufacturers contacted.

elements.quote: Authors or trial investigators for further information were contacted for queries pertaining to methodology, study outcome, availability of trial reports (if results not yet published as journal article).
elements.reason: Types of individuals contacted (authors or trial investigators) are explicitly described.

elements.quote: In addition, reference lists and bibliographies of previous systematic and non- systematic reviews were screened and citation tracking were undertaken to identify relevant studies.
elements.reason: The evidence specifies the kinds of reference lists examined (reference lists and bibliographies of previous systematic and non-systematic reviews).
Citation tracking is mentioned, but the seed reports, citation index/platform, and the search date are not reported.
No journals or conference proceedings consulted, dates covered, or search methods for them are reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Full search strategy has been provided as supplementary material (S1 Text). The trial may however be started before year 2000. Searches of published literature on effectiveness of NCD control interventions delivered through community health worker under the programme (focus on developing countries) were done in the following biomedical, and general reference electronic databases, without restriction to language: PubMed (20002015); Excerpta Medica Database (EMBASE) (2000-2015); OVID (2000-2015) and World PLOS Health Organization (WHO) library and Cochrane library.
elements.reason: The manuscript states that the full search strategy is provided in supplementary material (S1 Text) and names several sources/databases, but the complete, database-by-database search strings “as actually run” are not included in the retrieved evidence, so it cannot be confirmed for every source.

elements.reason: The evidence reports key search limits (publication years 2000–2015; no language restriction) and provides a rationale for limiting the time period, but it does not explicitly link all limits/filters to eligibility criteria “by reference” in a way that fully satisfies the requirement.
No information is provided in the retrieved evidence about citing published search approaches/filters or describing adaptations.

No peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) is described in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Due to the diversity of interventions and health topics covered, populations, study types and outcomes, a multi-stage search strategy was developed to identify relevant publications.
elements.reason: The retrieved evidence does not indicate that the search structure was “not based on PICO.” Instead, it describes a multi-stage strategy, so the specific requirement to report a final conceptual structure/explorations when not using PICO cannot be assessed as applicable based on the provided evidence.

elements.quote: For trials which had not accounted for clustering, sample size estimates were adjusted for design effect using an 'approximation method'.[27] Effective sample size was calculated for the comparison groups by dividing the original sample size by the design effect. Design effect was calculated as 1 + (M - 1) ICC, where M is the average cluster size and ICC is the intra-cluster correlation coefficient. If primary data was not provided, we attempted to find an appropriate ICC from the literature and adjusted the sample size accordingly.[28] ... Where the change per group was not available [26, 30], we used end-values where randomisation was successful.[26]
elements.reason: The manuscript describes multiple data preparation steps required before synthesis, including adjustments for missing clustering information (design effect/ICC and effective sample size) and substitution of end-values when change-per-group data were unavailable.

elements.quote: data or outcome were there, for which we contacted the study's primary author via email. elements.quote: The quality assessment represented as global score is included in the 'Characteristics of included studies' table. elements.quote: A major limitation observed was the low magnitude of effect and quality of evidence in study trials included in this review. A probable reason could have been the nature of studies (community based studies, as against controlled clinical settings) which dilutes the effect of interventions due to within subject and within cluster differences. Implementation of interventions by less trained staff could also have contributed to a decrease in effect size. With the exception of a trial by Jafar et al, all other included trials relied on short-term effects of interventions and failed to report issues related to behaviour relapse, as in interventions targeting medication adherence, weight loss or smoking. Also, shorter length of follow ups fail to capture 'saturation effects' of primary prevention interventions implemented at population level.[53] However, we found that on overall synthesis of results mean follow up for most of the outcomes was more than 12 months, which adds strength to the evidence. Minor and major methodological challenges in synthesising the evidence should also be understood while interpreting the results of this review.
